\title{Conditioning as Group Action:\\ Lie-Algebra Feature Modulation Composes\\ Where FiLM and Hypernetworks Memorize}
\author{Richard Bao\\ \texttt{richardbao419@gmail.com}}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\textbf{The finding, plainly:} if a network is conditioned by \emph{rotating} its features --- with
rotation angles that are a linear function of the condition --- then combined conditions produce
combined effects automatically, because rotations add; the network then handles combinations of
conditions it has never seen, which FiLM and even far more expensive hypernetwork conditioners
consistently fail at. Formally: Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) conditions a network by
scaling and shifting each feature independently, $y=\gamma(c)\odot x+\beta(c)$. We study its
natural generalization $y=\T(c)\,x+\beta(c)$ for structured, per-sample operators $\T(c)$, and
identify the single design choice that dominates compositional generalization: \emph{the condition
should enter the operator linearly in a Lie algebra}. Our conditioner, $\T(c)=P\,R(Wc)\,P^{\top}$ --- planar rotations with
angles linear in $c$, conjugated by a learned structured orthogonal basis $P$ --- satisfies
$\T(c_1{+}c_2)=\T(c_1)\T(c_2)$ \emph{exactly, by construction, for any weights}, so composition of
conditions is a property of the parametrization rather than something learned from data. Under a
pre-registered, budget-fair protocol (equal backbones, conditioning cost $\le$1.2$\times$ FiLM,
margins and statistical tests fixed before each run), we evaluate against FiLM, conditional
LayerNorm, concatenation, and two input-conditioned hypernetwork baselines on five compositional
benchmarks: two synthetic operator-learning suites and three image-transformation suites (dSprites
and 3D~Shapes) in which a conditioning operator must transform a \emph{learned} latent so that a
frozen-architecture decoder renders an image of a never-trained combination of factor changes.
\ours{} has the lowest compositional OOD error on all five suites --- by up to five orders of
magnitude when conditions form a group, and by 42.9--53.8\% over the strongest (43$\times$ more
expensive) hypernetwork baseline on image suites ($p{=}9.1\times10^{-5}$, Cliff's
$\delta{=}{-}1.0$, $N{=}10$ seeds) --- while using the fewest parameters of any conditioner, and
passes the full pre-registered gate on four of the five. On the fifth (3D~Shapes), the gate
returns a \emph{registered negative}: ours is still best on every compositional metric
(87.5\% below the strongest baseline; OOD/in-dist gap 1.13$\times$ vs.\ 13--26$\times$), but pays
a 1.46$\times$ in-distribution fit penalty that trips the pre-registered no-regression criterion
--- quantifying a real fit-vs-composition trade-off rather than hiding it. An ablation that swaps
only the linear angle map for an MLP --- same orthogonal basis, more compute --- degrades OOD
error by 1.5--43{,}000$\times$, isolating linearity-in-the-algebra as the mechanism.
Higher-capacity conditioners generalize \emph{worse}: compositional conditioning is an
inductive-bias problem, not a capacity problem.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Conditioning --- injecting a class, an action, a timestep, or a text embedding into a network's
computation --- is one of the most reused mechanisms in deep learning. Diffusion models modulate
every block on the timestep and class via adaLN \citep{peebles2023dit}; visual reasoning, speech,
and RL systems modulate features on questions, speakers, and goals \citep{perez2018film}; world
models condition latent dynamics on actions. Almost all of this conditioning is carried by three
mechanisms: concatenation, feature-wise affine modulation (FiLM), or a hypernetwork that emits
weights from the condition.

These mechanisms sit at two extremes of an expressivity axis. FiLM's diagonal transform is cheap
and stable but cannot rotate, mix, or exchange information between features. Hypernetworks can
express any linear operator but pay quadratic cost and, as we show, systematically \emph{memorize}
the training conditions: their error on novel combinations of familiar conditions is worse than
FiLM's, despite 43$\times$ the conditioning compute. The middle of this axis --- structured
operator families between diagonal and dense --- is well explored for \emph{weight} fine-tuning
(orthogonal and low-rank adapters: LoRA, OFT, BOFT, HRA
\citep{hu2022lora,qiu2023oft,liu2024boft,yuan2024hra}), but largely unexplored in FiLM's role:
\emph{per-sample, input-conditioned modulation of activations}.

We ask a sharp version of the question: \emph{which structure, at FiLM-level cost, buys
compositional generalization} --- correct behavior on combinations of conditions never seen
together in training? Our answer imports a mechanism from positional encoding. RoPE
\citep{su2021rope} and its generalization GRAPE \citep{grape2025} encode position $n$ as a group
action $G(n)=\exp(n\,\omega L)$: because position enters \emph{linearly in the Lie algebra}, the
relative law $G(n{+}m)=G(n)G(m)$ holds exactly. We transplant this construction from scalar
positions in attention to arbitrary condition vectors in activation modulation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:op}
y \;=\; \T(c)\,x+\beta(c), \qquad
\T(c) \;=\; P\; R(Wc)\; P^{\top},
\end{equation}
where $R(\theta)$ applies planar $2{\times}2$ rotations with angle vector $\theta$, $W$ is a
\emph{linear, bias-free} map from the condition into the angle space (the maximal torus of
$\mathrm{SO}(d)$), and $P$ is a learned orthogonal change of basis. Same-plane rotations commute,
so for any $W$ and $P$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:comp}
\T(c_1+c_2) \;=\; \T(c_1)\,\T(c_2),
\end{equation}
\emph{exactly, at every point in training}. Composition of conditions is not learned; it is a
theorem about the parametrization. The operator is exactly orthogonal (stable spectra), is the
identity at initialization and at $c=0$, and costs $1.11\times$ FiLM's conditioning FLOPs when $P$
is parametrized as a structured (Group-and-Shuffle style \citep{gorbunov2024gs}) orthogonal ---
a budget a \emph{dense} learned basis provably cannot meet (\S\ref{sec:budget}).

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\textbf{(1)} We formulate conditioning as a spectrum of per-sample structured operators
generalizing FiLM, positioned explicitly against the PEFT literature that owns these operator
families for \emph{weight} adaptation (\S\ref{sec:related}).
\textbf{(2)} We introduce \ours{} (Eq.~\ref{eq:op}), which makes condition composition exact by
construction at FiLM-class cost, including a budget analysis showing dense learned bases exceed
any FiLM-comparable FLOP ceiling while structured orthogonal bases fit (\S\ref{sec:method}).
\textbf{(3)} We contribute a pre-registered, budget-fair evaluation protocol --- margins,
statistical tests, and single-read OOD splits fixed before every run; equal-parameter,
equal-FLOP comparisons enforced by a shared counter --- and release it end-to-end
(\S\ref{sec:protocol}).
\textbf{(4)} Across five benchmarks we show: near machine-precision compositional generalization
and zero-shot extrapolation to longer compositions when conditions form a group; a robust
$\ge$2$\times$ advantage on real-image transformation with learned latents, surviving categorical
(non-group) factors; a mechanism-isolating ablation; interpretable learned rotations that recover
ground-truth generators to $2\times10^{-4}$ rad; and a consistent \emph{capacity inversion} ---
the more expressive the conditioner, the worse its compositional OOD (\S\ref{sec:results}).

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{FiLM and conditional normalization.} FiLM \citep{perez2018film} and its conditional
normalization variants (conditional BN/LN, adaLN in DiT \citep{peebles2023dit}) apply per-feature
affine transforms generated from a condition. All are diagonal: no feature mixing. We keep FiLM's
role --- per-sample activation modulation --- and enrich only the operator.

\paragraph{Structured operators in PEFT.} The operator families between diagonal and dense are
well studied as \emph{weight} fine-tuning: low-rank (LoRA \citep{hu2022lora}), block-diagonal
orthogonal (OFT \citep{qiu2023oft}), butterfly orthogonal (BOFT \citep{liu2024boft}), Householder
(HRA \citep{yuan2024hra}), block-orthogonal-with-permutations (Group-and-Shuffle
\citep{gorbunov2024gs}); \citet{he2022unified} give a unified view. These learn a \emph{fixed}
transform of weights per task. We claim no novelty for the operator families themselves; our
setting differs on every axis that matters --- per-sample, input-conditioned, activation-space,
and evaluated for compositional generation rather than task adaptation. Hypernetwork-generated
adapters (e.g., input-conditioned LoRA variants \citep{ha2017hypernetworks}) generate weights from
conditions but inherit the memorization behavior we quantify in \S\ref{sec:results}.

\paragraph{Position encodings as group actions.} RoPE \citep{su2021rope} rotates query/key pairs
by angles linear in position; GRAPE \citep{grape2025} generalizes this to group representations
$G(n)=\exp(n\omega L)$ with exact relative laws. The mechanism --- argument linear in a Lie
algebra, hence exact composition --- is theirs; our contribution is transplanting it from scalar
position in attention to arbitrary condition vectors in FiLM's role, learning the basis $P$, and
demonstrating budget-fair compositional gains there.

\paragraph{Compositional generalization in generative models.} \citet{montero2021role} showed
that reconstruction-trained generative models fail to render unseen factor combinations on
dSprites-class data, largely independent of disentanglement. Our image experiments adopt that
recombination paradigm but move the question to the \emph{conditioning mechanism}: with backbone,
data, and training identical, which operator family recombines? Symmetry-based representation
learning \citep{higgins2018towards,cohen2016group} argues latents should carry group actions; we
provide a conditioning-side mechanism and controlled evidence for it.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Conditioning as a structured operator}
FiLM is the diagonal case $\T(c)=\mathrm{diag}(1+\gamma(c))$ of $y=\T(c)x+\beta(c)$. We require of
any richer $\T(c)$: \textbf{(i) identity at init} ($\T\equiv I$, $\beta\equiv0$), so the
conditioned model starts as the unconditioned one; \textbf{(ii) bounded spectrum}
($\sigma_{\max}(\T(c))\approx1$), so modulation cannot blow up activations; \textbf{(iii)
compositionality} --- ideally $\T(c_1{+}c_2)=\T(c_1)\T(c_2)$; \textbf{(iv) FiLM-class cost}. All
four are unit-tested properties of our released implementation.

\subsection{\ours{}: the condition enters linearly in the Lie algebra}
In Eq.~\ref{eq:op}, $W\in\mathbb{R}^{(d/2)\times k}$ is linear with no bias, so $c=0$ gives
$\T=I$, and $W{=}0$ at initialization gives identity-init. $R(\theta)$ rotates coordinate pairs
$(x_{2i},x_{2i+1})$ by $\theta_i$ --- the maximal torus of $\mathrm{SO}(d)$, applied in
closed form (no matrix exponential at runtime).

\begin{proposition}
For any $W,P$ and any $c_1,c_2$: $\T(c_1+c_2)=\T(c_1)\T(c_2)$, and $\T(c)^{\top}\T(c)=I$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$R(\theta_1)R(\theta_2)=R(\theta_1{+}\theta_2)$ since coordinate-pair rotations act on disjoint
planes; $W$ linear gives $W(c_1{+}c_2)=Wc_1{+}Wc_2$; conjugation by a fixed $P$ preserves both
products. Orthogonality: $R$ and $P$ are orthogonal.
\end{proof}

The point of the construction is what it removes: an MLP head from $c$ to angles (or to any
operator parameters) must \emph{learn} composition from data and extrapolate it to unseen
combinations. Here composition holds at initialization, during training, and off-distribution.
The learned parts --- $W$'s columns (a generator per condition dimension) and the basis $P$ ---
only determine \emph{which} planes and \emph{how fast} each condition dimension rotates them.

\subsection{The basis must be structured: a budget analysis}
\label{sec:budget}
$\T(c)$ must act in the right basis: a coordinate-aligned torus fails whenever the data's factors
mix coordinates (S2 below shows this collapse). A \emph{dense} learned orthogonal $P$ costs two
$d{\times}d$ matrix--vector products per sample --- $4d^2$ FLOPs, i.e.\ $1.52\times$ FiLM's entire
conditioning budget at $d{=}128$, before counting anything else. (An early version of our own
accounting under-counted this by $2\times$; the corrected counter is a regression-tested part of
the release, and the erratum is documented in the repository.) We therefore parametrize $P$ as
$L{=}5$ layers of block-diagonal orthogonal matrices (eight $16{\times}16$ Cayley blocks per
layer, $Q=(I{+}A)^{-1}(I{-}A)$ for skew $A$, exactly orthogonal, identity at $A{=}0$) with fixed
permutations between layers, in the spirit of BOFT and Group-and-Shuffle
\citep{liu2024boft,gorbunov2024gs}. Total conditioning cost: $1.11\times$ FiLM FLOPs, with $P$
undercomplete (4{,}800 parameters vs.\ $\dim\mathrm{SO}(128)=8{,}128$) --- it need only discover
the planes the conditions act on, not an arbitrary rotation.

\section{Pre-registered, budget-fair protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

\paragraph{Arms.} Six conditioners share one condition encoder and differ only in the operator:
FiLM; Concat-MLP; conditional LayerNorm; \textbf{Hypernetwork} ($\T=I{+}\Delta W(c)$, dense);
\textbf{Dynamic low-rank} ($\T=I{+}A(c)B(c)^{\top}$, per-sample LoRA-style); and \ours{}. A
seventh reported (never gated) arm isolates the mechanism: identical structured $P$, but an MLP
angle head replacing $W$ --- \emph{more} compute than ours, differing only in linearity.

\paragraph{Fairness.} A single shared counter measures trainable parameters and per-sample
forward FLOPs of the whole conditioning path. Gates: ours must hold $\le1.05\times$ the smallest
hypernetwork baseline's parameters and $\le1.20\times$ FiLM's FLOPs; unstructured baselines may be
arbitrarily larger (they are: up to 48$\times$ our parameters). Table~\ref{tab:budget} reports the
budgets. All arms share identical backbones, optimizers, schedules, seeds, and (for image suites)
identical evaluation triplets.

\paragraph{Pre-registration.} For every suite, the success margin, significance test, seed count,
and split protocol were written down before the run: verdict = win only if ours beats the
\emph{strongest hypernetwork-family} baseline (not merely FiLM --- beating a diagonal operator on
rotation-bearing tasks would be nearly tautological) by $\ge$20\% relative OOD error, one-sided
Mann--Whitney $p\le0.01$ and Cliff's $|\delta|\ge0.474$ over $N{=}10$ seeds, at fair budget, with
no in-distribution regression. Model selection uses a validation split; each OOD test split is
evaluated once per trained arm. Deviations (two pre-run amendments; one accounting erratum) are
disclosed in the repository alongside append-only logs sufficient to recompute every statistic.

\paragraph{Benchmarks.} \textbf{S1 (synthetic, aligned):} inputs $x\in\mathbb{R}^{128}$; a
multi-hot condition over $K{=}8$ primitive block-plane rotations requests $y=M(c)x$; train on
singletons + 8 pairs, test on 10 held-out pairs. \textbf{S2 (synthetic, hidden basis):}
identical, but $M(c)=B\,R(c)\,B^{\top}$ for a fixed random orthonormal $B$ --- the operator is
\emph{not} handed the data's basis and must discover it; we additionally evaluate all 56
never-trained \emph{triple} compositions. \textbf{S3 (dSprites):} conditional image
transformation. Encode a real image $x_1$, apply the conditioning arm for a factor-change
$\Delta$ over \{scale, orientation, position$_x$, position$_y$\}, decode, and score pixel MSE
against the \emph{ground-truth} image at the shifted factors (dSprites \citep{matthey2017dsprites}
is a deterministic factor$\to$image map, so compositional generation is objectively scoreable).
Train on single-factor changes + 2 of 6 two-factor types; OOD-test on 2 never-trained two-factor
types; report never-trained three-factor types. \textbf{S3b (dSprites + categorical):} adds shape
change --- a factor that is \emph{not} a one-parameter group --- encoded as a one-hot difference
(which still adds). \textbf{S4 (3D Shapes):} the same protocol on RGB, 3D-rendered scenes
\citep{burgess2018shapes} with six factors (three cyclic hues, scale, orientation, and categorical
shape), $\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{9}$.

\paragraph{When conditions form a group, composition is solved, not approximated (S1--S2).}
On the hidden-basis suite, ours reaches $3.3\times10^{-8}$ OOD MSE --- five orders of magnitude
below the strongest baseline (Table~\ref{tab:main}) --- and, on the 56 never-trained
\emph{triples}, $5.3\times10^{-8}$: error does not grow with composition length
(Fig.~\ref{fig:length}, left). The composition identity (Eq.~\ref{eq:comp}) holds on trained
models to $6.7\times10^{-6}$ (Frobenius). A coordinate-aligned ablation ($P{=}I$) collapses to
FiLM's error --- basis discovery, not hand-alignment, carries the result --- and the learned
angles match the ground-truth generators to $2\times10^{-4}$ rad (Fig.~\ref{fig:length}, right):
one interpretable rotation plane per primitive.

\paragraph{The advantage survives learned latents and real images (S3--S4).}
On dSprites transformation, all arms fit in-distribution identically ($\approx1.4\times10^{-3}$
pixel MSE) --- the comparison isolates composition by construction --- yet ours is the only arm
whose OOD/in-dist ratio stays near 1 (1.25$\times$ vs.\ 2.1--3.3$\times$ for all baselines;
Table~\ref{tab:ratio}), beating the strongest baseline by 53.8\% at 39$\times$ fewer conditioning
FLOPs. Never-trained three-factor changes degrade ours most gracefully (1.48$\times$ its own
in-dist).

\paragraph{Categorical factors attenuate but do not break the advantage (S3b).}
Adding shape change --- a factor with no one-parameter group structure, encoded as a one-hot
difference --- attenuates the margin exactly as the theory predicts (exact composition no longer
covers every factor), yet the pre-registered gate still passes decisively: 42.9\% over the
strongest baseline ($p{=}9.1\times10^{-5}$, complete seed separation), with a compositional gap
of 1.63$\times$ vs.\ 2.4--3.2$\times$ for every baseline (Table~\ref{tab:ratio}). The linear map
simply assigns each categorical transition its own rotation, sacrificing exactness on the
categorical dimension while preserving it on the geometric ones. The capacity inversion persists
here too (hypernetwork 2.87$\times$, dynamic low-rank 3.23$\times$, both worse than FiLM's
2.41$\times$).

\paragraph{S4 (3D Shapes): the gate fires a registered negative --- and quantifies the trade-off.}
\label{sec:s4kill}
On RGB, 3D-rendered scenes with six factors, ours again has the best compositional metrics by a
wide margin: OOD error 87.5\% below the strongest baseline (complete seed separation), OOD/in-dist
gap 1.13$\times$ vs.\ 13.1$\times$ (hypernetwork) and 26.1$\times$ (dynamic low-rank), and the
flattest degradation on never-trained three-factor changes. Nevertheless, the pre-registered
verdict for this suite is \emph{negative}: our in-distribution error ($1.03\times10^{-3}$) is
1.46$\times$ the best memorizer's ($7.1\times10^{-4}$), violating the registered no-regression
criterion ($\le$1.10$\times$) that exists precisely to prevent buying OOD robustness by
under-fitting. We report the verdict as registered. The reading we defend: on richer scenes the
exact-orthogonality constraint has a measurable in-distribution price, and whether that price is
worth an 8$\times$ OOD improvement is application-dependent --- a trade-off our protocol surfaces
with numbers where a less constrained evaluation would have simply declared victory. (Two
baselines' small ratios in Table~\ref{tab:ratio} are artifacts of poor fits inflating the
denominator: Concat-MLP and Cond-LN fit 4--7$\times$ worse in-distribution than the memorizers.)
\footnote{All suite cells are generated from the same pre-registered pipeline; per-suite verdicts
and append-only logs are in the repository.}

\paragraph{The mechanism is the linearity, and capacity actively hurts.}
The ablation shares our orthogonal basis and exceeds our compute; it differs \emph{only} in
replacing the linear angle map with an MLP. It is 43{,}000$\times$ worse on synthetic triples and
1.55$\times$ worse on dSprites OOD. Meanwhile the two hypernetwork-family arms --- the only arms
that can represent \emph{any} conditioning operator --- have the \emph{worst} compositional gaps
on images (2.7$\times$ and 3.3$\times$) despite 6--43$\times$ the FLOPs: they spend capacity
memorizing training condition-types. Compositional conditioning is an inductive-bias problem;
adding expressivity moves it in the wrong direction.

\section{Limitations and scope}
Learned latents do not support exact group action: the real-image advantage is a robust
$\approx$2$\times$, not the synthetic suites' $10^{5}\times$, and Eq.~\ref{eq:comp} holding in the
operator does not force the encoder--decoder pair to respect it. S4 shows the constraint can
carry a real in-distribution cost (1.46$\times$ the best memorizer) on richer scenes --- our own
gate scores that suite as a negative --- so exact orthogonality should be understood as a
robustness--fit trade-off, not a free lunch; relaxations (orthogonal $\times$ bounded low-rank)
are the obvious next design point. Our images are controlled
64$\times$64 benchmarks with known factors; natural-image, text-conditioned, and diffusion-scale
evaluations (the natural deployment is the adaLN site in DiT blocks) are future work, as is
conditioning at multiple depths. Conditions whose semantics are far from any group action ---
open-ended text, unordered categories at large cardinality --- may need hybrid operators
(orthogonal $\times$ low-rank), which our framework accommodates but this paper does not evaluate
at scale.

\section{Reproducibility statement}
Every experiment was pre-registered (margins, tests, splits fixed before running; specifications
in the repository), runs from a single command per suite, and writes append-only logs from which
every number in this paper --- all tables and figures are generated directly from those logs ---
can be recomputed. Property tests pin the operator invariants (identity-init, orthogonality,
bounded spectrum, exact composition) and the fairness counters. We additionally disclose two
pre-run amendments (training loss on sparse binary images; step count) and one corrected FLOP
accounting erratum, with the corrected counter regression-tested.
